faq.a: A model that keeps learning changes its behaviour after validation, which makes it hard to prove it still performs as tested. Locked models can be validated and changed under change control.

title: Manufacturing and Supply Chain
answer: AI in manufacturing is moving from pilots to regulated use: models monitor processes, inspect product visually and predict equipment failure, and drugmakers are building digital twins of their plants. Europe's draft GMP Annex 22 is the first rule set written for AI in medicine manufacturing.

reading.body:
AI in pharmaceutical manufacturing is shifting from pilots to regulated use, with Europe's draft GMP Annex 22 the first rule set written specifically for it.

The pattern is a move from advisory to automated. Models monitor processes, inspect product visually, predict equipment failure, and simulate plants as digital twins. The draft Annex 22, published for consultation in July 2025, sets out how models used in manufacturing must be validated and overseen. The FDA's draft AI credibility guidance, from January 2025, applies whenever a model produces data supporting a quality decision, which covers manufacturing as well as clinical work.

The practical consequence is that validation, not model capability, sets the pace. A static, locked model is far easier to validate than one that keeps learning, so the near-term path runs through uses where the AI advises and a person decides, such as anomaly alerts and predictive maintenance, before automated release. Roche's use of NVIDIA Omniverse to build digital twins of production lines shows the compute layer reaching the plant floor, but the constraint on scaling these systems is regulatory rather than computational.

What this does not cover is cost, throughput, or how many manufacturers have actually deployed any of it. The data names one company and two regulatory documents, so it describes the direction of travel and the rules being written for it, not adoption rates or measured results.

siblings.name: AI Adoption and Governance in Life Sciences

explainer:
Making medicines is tightly controlled because quality cannot be tested into a product at the end; it has to be built into every step. Plants operate under Good Manufacturing Practice, every critical process is validated, and every batch has a documented record reviewed before release. Any computerised system that affects product quality must itself be validated and its data kept with full integrity.

AI fits naturally into this environment because plants generate continuous streams of process, equipment and quality data. Typical uses include vision systems that inspect tablets, vials and packaging; models that predict equipment failure before it stops a line; analytics that spot process drift early; models that predict stability and shelf life; and digital twins that simulate a process or a whole line before changes are made on the floor. Continuous manufacturing, where material flows through without stopping between steps, depends on exactly this kind of real time monitoring and control.

The constraint is validation. Regulators prefer AI that is locked once in production, tested on independent data against criteria set in advance, and overseen by people where it is not fully reliable. Europe's draft Annex 22 states these expectations most directly, and the FDA's credibility framework and data integrity rules apply in the United States.

Most companies start where AI advises and a person decides, such as maintenance alerts, then move to quality critical uses once data pipelines and validation methods are proven.
key_points: GMP requires validated systems and complete data integrity, including for AI.
Main uses: visual inspection, predictive maintenance, process monitoring, stability prediction, digital twins.
Continuous manufacturing relies on real time AI monitoring and control.
Regulators favour locked models tested on independent data with predefined criteria.
Start with advisory uses, then extend to quality critical ones.
